summary: Iran claims mined tankers burned in Hormuz as a US envoy urges a pause, Likud alleges fraud in Israel, a drone kills 14 in Dnipro, Spain mourns a rail crash and Lagarde will leave the ECB.

topics.heading: Iran says three tankers hit mines in Hormuz as a US envoy calls for a 'time out'
topics.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz; no one has confirmed it. The same day, a US envoy said the two sides were close to an initial understanding.[^1][^2]

lead.title: Middle East war: Iran claims tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO confirms strike off Oman; fired US general reportedly admitted Iran leaks

alsoReported.title: Iran Says Three Oil Tankers Caught Fire After Hitting Mines in Strait of Hormuz
Qatari mediators hand Iran new proposal to end the war

article: Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said on Thursday that three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines while leaving the Strait of Hormuz by what Iran calls an "unauthorised" southern route[^1][^2]. The IRGC says the ships had switched off their radar and navigation systems and ignored warnings, but it did not name them or say which flags they flew[^2]. The claim could not be independently confirmed[^1][^2]. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO), which tracks shipping incidents, confirmed that a tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile near Khasab, Oman, with no injuries reported; it did not say who fired it[^1].

Background: Iran has restricted traffic through the strait, a narrow channel that carries a large share of the world's oil, since the war began on February 28, and the US has blockaded Iranian ports[^2]. The US military estimates the war had cost it at least $47.1 billion by mid-October, most of it to replace munitions[^3].

Diplomacy is moving at the same time. US envoy Tom Barrack told CNN that both sides should take "a time out" to bring temperatures down, and said they were "very close" to an initial understanding, crediting Qatar and Pakistan as mediators[^1]. Iran confirmed it had received a letter from Vice President JD Vance but had not replied[^1]. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran's seven conditions must be agreed first and that pressure would not work[^1]. Earlier in the week, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that ideas brought by Qatari mediators were "unacceptable"[^3].
The war also has other fronts. Saudi Arabia says it intercepted two ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthis toward Riyadh, with falling debris injuring one person[^1].

Why it matters: mines are hard to find and slow to clear, so even an unconfirmed claim can make shipowners more cautious and keep oil prices high, which is what has pushed up fuel and food costs in Canada. My read: a public call for a pause and new ship incidents on the same day show how unsettled things are before the US midterms on November 3.
topics.differences: Iran says the tankers ignored its warnings and used an unauthorised route[^2]. No independent source has confirmed the mine strikes, and UKMTO has not linked its projectile report to Iran[^1]. A US envoy describes the sides as close to an understanding, while Iran's parliament speaker says its own conditions must come first[^1].

topics.heading: Netanyahu's Likud claims Arab-led parties 'stole' Israel's election; panel reviews it
topics.summary: After Arab-led parties won a record share of seats and neither bloc reached a majority, Likud alleged widespread fraud. It has not published proof, and the election committee says it is reviewing the request.[^4]

lead.title: Likud claims election 'stolen' by Arab parties following their record performance

alsoReported.title: Qatari mediators hand Iran new proposal to end the war

article: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party said on Wednesday that Israel's October 27 election had been "stolen" by Arab-led parties, and asked the police and the Shin Bet security service to investigate alleged widespread fraud and voter intimidation[^4]. Likud says it handed over "hundreds of testimonies" and other evidence, including claims about illegal software used to get voters out[^4]. It has not made that evidence public. Hours earlier, an official at the Central Elections Committee had dismissed fraud claims in a TV interview; the committee now says it is reviewing Likud's request[^4].

The background is the count. With more than 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's bloc had 53 seats and Gadi Eisenkot and his partners 48, while the Joint List (12) and Ra'am (7) were on course for a record 19 seats, nearly double their current 10[^4]. Forming a government takes 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats[^4]. Before the vote, both Netanyahu and the opposition had said they would not form a government that relies on Arab parties[^3].

That arithmetic makes the Arab-led parties possible kingmakers. Joint List chair Yousef Jabareen told AFP his party does not see itself joining a coalition under current conditions, but that anyone offering an alternative to Netanyahu "will have to talk to us"[^4]. Ra'am says it wants to be part of the next government, and Democrats leader Yair Golan urged opposition parties to drop their pledges against working with the Arab-led lists[^4].

Why it matters: the result decides who leads Israel on Gaza, Iran and relations with the US, and the dispute touches an old question in Israeli politics about whether Arab citizens' parties can be partners in government. My read: a fraud claim made before evidence is shown can shape how people see the result, whatever an investigation later finds. Next comes the final count, then coalition talks that could take weeks.
topics.differences: Likud says it has evidence of fraud and intimidation and wants police and the Shin Bet to investigate[^4]. An election committee official had earlier dismissed fraud claims, and the committee says it is now reviewing Likud's request[^4]. No evidence has been made public so far.

topics.heading: Russian drone strike on a busy Dnipro railway platform kills at least 14
topics.summary: A Russian drone hit a crowded platform at Dnipro's main station on Thursday, killing at least 14 people, Ukrainian officials say. It came as a small local truce held for a third day and new talks were planned for next month.[^5][^6]

lead.title: Russian drone strike kills at least 14 on Ukrainian rail platform

alsoReported.title: Russian drone attack on train station kills 13 in Ukraine's Dnipro

article: A Russian drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in Dnipro, a large city in eastern-central Ukraine, on Thursday, killing at least 14 people, according to the regional governor, Oleksandr Hanzha[^5][^6]. Another 14 were wounded, six seriously, among them an 11-year-old boy[^5]. The state rail company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a jet-powered drone struck the platform where a commuter train was preparing to leave for Zaporizhzhia, and that people were there despite a danger warning[^6].

Ukraine's air force said it shot down three jet-powered drones in the daytime attack, but a fourth got through[^5]. Officials reported other deaths the same day, including two 15-year-old girls in Chernihiv and three people in Kremenchuk[^5]. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike "horrific" and said sanctions on Russia must not be eased while the war continues, criticising a deal this month between Presidents Trump and Putin that eased some sanctions so Russia could release diesel[^5]. French President Emmanuel Macron said it was intolerable that Russia keeps rejecting proposals to stop the fighting[^5].

Background: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and there is still no general ceasefire. A small local truce around Russian-occupied Oleshky, in the Kherson region, entered its third day on Thursday so that aid could get in[^5]. Russia and Ukraine are due to meet US envoys next month to restart talks, but no firm dates have been set[^5].

Why it matters: railways move people, grain and aid across a country at war, so strikes on stations hit daily life far from the front. My read: a deadly strike in the same week as a local truce shows how small the current steps toward peace are; next month's talks will test whether that changes.

topics.heading: Spain's second deadly high-speed rail crash this year kills at least 68 near Toledo
topics.summary: A high-speed train hit a stopped train near Urda, south of Madrid, killing at least 68 people by the regional count (69 in other reports). Investigators are looking at a signalling failure and an order from a control centre.[^7][^8][^9]

lead.title: What we know about Spain's second high-speed rail tragedy this year

alsoReported.title: Spain train crash: What happened in the 17 minutes before the collision?
'Inexplicable' order probed as cause of train crash that killed at least 69: Official

article: A high-speed train ran into the back of a stopped train near Urda, in Toledo province south of Madrid, on Wednesday morning. The Castilla-La Mancha regional government says at least 68 people were killed; other reports put the toll at 69[^7][^9]. About 80 people were injured, about 15 of them critically, according to regional president Emiliano García-Page[^7]. A Renfe train with 397 passengers hit a stationary Iryo train carrying 147, and two Iryo carriages left the track[^7][^8].

How it happened is under investigation. At about 8:30 a.m., a computer failure knocked out LZB, the automatic train-control system, along about 63 km of the Madrid-Seville line, stopping six trains[^8]. Controllers at Madrid's Atocha centre then let trains move again using trackside signals. The Iryo driver reported that her train was still stuck, but, according to El País, the Renfe train was not told to stop before the collision at 8:53 a.m.[^7][^8]. Transport Minister Óscar Puente called a control-centre order "inexplicable" and said the drivers were not to blame[^7][^9]. A court in Orgaz has taken over the judicial inquiry and ordered the trains' black boxes seized[^8].

It is Spain's second deadly high-speed crash this year: a collision near Adamuz in January killed 46[^7]. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared three days of national mourning and called two such accidents in one year "unacceptable"[^7]. Renfe has suspended ticket sales on the Madrid-Andalusia corridor until December 13, and about 1,500 people protested at the transport ministry calling for Puente to resign[^7].

Why it matters: high-speed rail relies on layers of safety, so that one failure does not become a disaster. My read: the key question here is less about the trains than about how people and computers hand control to each other when a system goes down, a lesson for any automated safety system.

topics.heading: The ECB holds rates at 2.5% as Christine Lagarde says she will step down in February
topics.summary: The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5% while fighting an oil-driven rise in inflation, and its president, Christine Lagarde, said she will leave on February 7, 2027, months before her term ends.[^10][^11]

lead.title: ECB President Christine Lagarde to step down next February, months before her mandate ends

alsoReported.title: ECB President Lagarde announces resignation after months of speculation
ECB President Lagarde to step down on 7 February 2027

article: The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro, kept its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday[^11][^12]. On the same day, its president, Christine Lagarde, announced that she will step down on February 7, 2027, about nine months before her eight-year term was due to end[^10][^11].

Lagarde, 70, said she wants "greater freedom" to give her views and work on issues beyond monetary policy, and that she "cannot remain neutral"[^11]. The bank gave no other reason[^11]. The decision drew criticism from Jean-Philippe Tanguy, an economics adviser in Marine Le Pen's French party, who called it "another insult", and from German member of the European Parliament Markus Ferber, who said it sent "the wrong signal"[^12]. Others, such as economist Marcel Fratzscher, praised her sense of responsibility toward Europe[^12].

Background: like the central banks in Ottawa and Washington, the ECB is facing higher inflation driven by the oil shock from the Iran war, and it has been raising rates[^12]. An economist quoted by Reuters sees "a low bar" for another hike in December, and money markets expect the deposit rate to reach 3.25% by the end of next year[^12]. European Council President António Costa says the search for a successor will start without delay; names mentioned include Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot of the Netherlands[^11].

Why it matters: the ECB decides what borrowing costs for households and businesses across much of Europe, in the middle of an energy shock. My read: a change at the top during a rate-hiking cycle adds some uncertainty, but ECB decisions are taken by its whole Governing Council, so policy is unlikely to swing on one person's departure.

topics.heading: Google releases Gemini 4 Carbon, a cyber-defence AI model, to selected users first
topics.summary: Google unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon, an AI model it says leads at finding and fixing software flaws. Because those skills could also help attackers, it is going first only to selected cyber defenders.[^13][^14]

lead.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon AI model with cybersecurity focus

alsoReported.title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon Can Find and Exploit Software Flaws. Who Gets Access?

article: Google on Wednesday unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon, a new frontier AI model that it says performs at the top level on cybersecurity tasks such as finding software flaws, exploiting them and writing fixes[^13]. It came two weeks after the company's Gemini 4 Argon model[^13]. Unlike most launches, Carbon is going first only to a selected group of cyber defenders through Google's Fairwind Program[^13][^14].

Google reports scores of 88.2% on a test of finding vulnerabilities, 54.8% on a test of exploiting them and 71% on writing working fixes, and says it ran these tests with safety guardrails switched off to measure the model's raw ability[^14]. It also says Carbon writes secure code at more than twice Argon's success rate[^13]. Fairwind members must limit which employees can use it and use multi-factor login, and Google says it takes part in voluntary pre-release testing with the US government[^14]. Prices start at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens[^13].

Background: a model that is good at finding security holes is "dual-use". Defenders can patch flaws before criminals find them, but attackers could use the same skill, which is why Google is limiting access. Independent testers at Artificial Analysis ranked Carbon first on their general intelligence index, but also found that its rate of made-up answers on one test rose from 4% for Argon to 11%[^14].

Why it matters: AI labs increasingly release their most capable models in stages, starting with trusted users, while governments argue over safety rules. My read: staged releases are a real safety step, but they rest on each company's own choices about who gets access, and most of the performance numbers so far come from Google itself.

question.text: Today Iran says mines set three tankers on fire, and Likud says an election was stolen. Neither claim has been confirmed. What kind of evidence would convince you either way, and who would you trust to check it?

read.title: Spain train crash: What happened in the 17 minutes before the collision?
read.summary: A minute-by-minute account of how a signalling failure, radio calls and control-centre decisions led to Spain's deadly train collision. A clear case study in how safety systems fail.
